concepts.title: Recall@k and Precision@k as Retrieval Metrics
concepts.description: Recall@k already showed up earlier in this subject as a way to check an approximate index against a brute-force baseline; this concept introduces a related but genuinely different pair of metrics -- recall@k and precision@k measured against human-judged relevance -- for answering a completely different question: not 'did the ANN index find what exact search would have found,' but 'is this retrieval system actually useful to the people relying on it.'
learningObjectives: Distinguish ANN recall@k (approximate index vs. brute-force ground truth) from information-retrieval recall@k (retrieval system vs. human-judged relevance), and explain why the same term means genuinely different things in each context.
Define and compute precision@k and recall@k given a ranked list of retrieved ids and a set of truly relevant ids.
Explain the precision/recall tension as k changes, and predict how each metric tends to move as k grows.
Explain the precision@k ceiling effect that occurs when the total number of truly relevant items is smaller than k, and why it doesn't indicate a flawed retriever.
Identify why using a retrieval system's own similarity scores as its relevance ground truth is a circular, meaningless evaluation, and explain what an independent ground truth requires instead.

sections.heading: Two Different 'Recall@k's -- Disambiguating a Reused Term
sections.body:
This subject already used the term 'recall@k' once before, in the concept on indexing parameters and the speed/accuracy tradeoff -- and it's worth being explicit that this concept's recall@k, while computed with an identical-looking formula, is answering a fundamentally different question, because the two use *different ground truths*.

The earlier, **ANN recall@k** compares an approximate index's top-k results against what an *exact, brute-force search over the same embeddings* would have returned. It's a measure of algorithmic fidelity: how well does the fast, approximate method reproduce the exact method's answer, for a fixed embedding model and a fixed notion of similarity? A recall@10 of 0.97 in that context says 'HNSW or IVF found 97% of what brute-force cosine similarity search would have found for this query,' and it says nothing at all about whether brute-force cosine similarity search itself was actually returning *useful* or *relevant* results in any human sense.

This concept's **retrieval-quality recall@k** compares the system's top-k results -- run through the *entire* pipeline, embeddings and ANN index and any filtering all included -- against a set of documents a human (or some other trusted, independent judgment process) has determined are actually relevant to that specific query. A recall@10 of 0.97 in *this* context says something completely different: '97% of the documents a human said were genuinely relevant to this query ended up in the system's top 10 results.' Confusing these two is an easy, consequential mistake -- a system can have excellent ANN recall (its approximate index faithfully reproduces exact search) while having terrible retrieval-quality recall (because the embeddings themselves, or the chunking, or the filtering, are steering exact search toward the wrong documents in the first place). ANN recall measures whether the *algorithm* is doing its job; retrieval-quality recall measures whether the *system* is doing its job -- and a perfect score on the first tells you nothing about the second.

sections.heading: Precision@k and Recall@k, Defined and Computed
sections.body:
With that disambiguation in place, the two metrics this concept is actually about are refreshingly simple to define, given a ranked list of retrieved ids and a set of ids a human has judged genuinely relevant to the query:

**Precision@k**: of the k items the system actually returned, what fraction are truly relevant? It answers 'how much of what I got back is actually useful?'

**Recall@k**: of *all* the truly relevant items that exist anywhere in the collection for this query, what fraction made it into the top k? It answers 'how much of what I should have gotten did I actually get?'

```python
def precision_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k):
    top_k = retrieved[:k]
    hits = sum(1 for item in top_k if item in relevant)
    return hits / k

def recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k):
    top_k = retrieved[:k]
    hits = sum(1 for item in top_k if item in relevant)
    return hits / len(relevant)

relevant_ids = {"docA", "docC", "docF", "docH"}
retrieved_ids = ["docA", "docB", "docC", "docD", "docF"]

for k in (1, 3, 5):
    print(k, round(precision_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, k), 3), round(recall_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, k), 3))
```

Notice the denominators are different by design: precision divides by `k` (what you actually looked at), while recall divides by `len(relevant)` (everything that was ever truly relevant, whether or not it was retrieved at all). This is exactly why recall requires knowing the *complete* set of relevant items for a query ahead of time -- an omniscient piece of information a real system doesn't have access to at query time, which is precisely what the golden dataset in the next concept exists to supply, curated ahead of time specifically so this metric can be computed at all.

sections.heading: The Precision/Recall Tension, and the Ceiling Effect
sections.body:
Running the same query through both metrics at increasing values of k reveals a real, structural tension: **recall@k is monotonically non-decreasing in k** -- fetching more results can only ever add more relevant items to what you've retrieved (or leave the count unchanged), never remove one, so recall@k never gets worse as k grows. **Precision@k has no such guarantee** -- it depends entirely on whether the *additional* items pulled in as k grows happen to be relevant or not, and can go up, down, or stay flat as k increases, depending on exactly where the relevant items happen to rank.

This creates a genuine design tension that shows up constantly in practice: a RAG pipeline choosing how many chunks to stuff into an LLM's context window is implicitly choosing a point on this same tradeoff -- a larger k tends toward higher recall (less chance of missing the one chunk that actually contains the answer) but risks lower precision (more irrelevant chunks diluting the context and, per the metadata-filtering-and-RAG concept earlier in this subject, giving a capable model more opportunity to confidently synthesize an answer from irrelevant surrounding material). There's no universally 'correct' k -- the right choice depends on how the retrieved results are actually being used downstream, which is a product decision informed by, but not fully determined by, these two metrics.

A specific edge case is worth calling out explicitly because it trips people up: if a query genuinely has fewer relevant documents in the entire collection than k -- say only 2 relevant documents exist, but you're computing precision@10 -- then **no retriever, however good, can ever achieve a precision@10 above 0.2**, because there simply aren't 10 relevant items available to fill the top 10 with. This is the **precision ceiling effect**, and it means precision@k has to be interpreted in light of how many relevant items actually exist for that query, not treated as an absolute quality bar independent of it -- a 'low' precision@10 might mean a mediocre retriever, or it might mean a perfectly good retriever facing a query that just doesn't have 10 good answers available anywhere in the collection.

sections.heading: Two Ways to Corrupt the Measurement Without Realizing It
sections.body:
Two specific mistakes turn these metrics from a genuine signal into a number that looks reassuring but measures nothing real, and both are worth guarding against explicitly.

The first is **circular evaluation**: computing 'relevance' from the retrieval system's own output -- for instance, treating whatever the system's top-k similarity search already returned as the relevant set, then checking whether the system's own top-k matches it. This isn't a shortcut, it's a tautology: a system's output trivially matches itself with perfect precision and recall every single time, regardless of whether the results are actually good, bad, or nonsensical -- the score can't distinguish a genuinely excellent retriever from a genuinely broken one, because both would score identically perfect against ground truth derived from their own output. Relevance judgments have to come from a source genuinely independent of the system being measured -- a human, a separate trusted process, or (with real caution, discussed in the next concept) a different, carefully-checked model -- never from the system's own similarity scores.

The second is **evaluation/production mismatch**: computing recall@k or precision@k using an unfiltered top-k, when real production queries always apply metadata filters (tenant scope, permissions, soft-delete exclusion) on top of the raw similarity search. A test harness that measures against the pure, unfiltered ANN results is measuring a system that doesn't actually exist in production -- and given everything covered in the metadata-filtering concepts of the previous module, filtering can change which documents actually make it into the top k in ways that matter a great deal. An evaluation that doesn't apply the same filters real queries would apply is optimistic by construction, and the gap between that optimistic number and reality only shows up once real, filtered traffic hits the system.

examples.title: Computing Precision@k and Recall@k as k Grows
examples.explanation: Four documents are genuinely relevant to this query (docA, docC, docF, docH), and the system's ranked results are docA, docB, docC, docD, docF -- notice docH, one of the truly relevant documents, never appears in this ranked list at all. At k=1, only docA is in view, which is relevant, giving perfect precision (1.0) but low recall (1/4 = 0.25, since 3 of the 4 relevant documents haven't been seen yet). At k=3, docB (irrelevant) has entered the picture alongside docA and docC (both relevant), dropping precision to 2/3 (about 0.667) while recall climbs to 2/4 (0.5). At k=5, docF (relevant) joins the mix, pushing recall up further to 3/4 (0.75), while precision settles at 3/5 (0.6). Recall only ever goes up as k grows (0.25 -> 0.5 -> 0.75) because relevant items already found are never un-found, but precision moves around based on exactly what else got pulled in at each step -- and recall can never reach 1.0 here no matter how large k gets, because docH was never retrieved by this system at all.

examples.title: The Precision Ceiling: A 'Perfect' Retriever Can Still Score Low Precision@10
examples.code:
def precision_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k):
    top_k = retrieved[:k]
    hits = sum(1 for item in top_k if item in relevant)
    return hits / k

def recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k):
    top_k = retrieved[:k]
    hits = sum(1 for item in top_k if item in relevant)
    return hits / len(relevant)

relevant_ids = {"x1", "x2"}   # only 2 documents in the ENTIRE collection are relevant to this query
retrieved_ids = ["x1", "x2", "y1", "y2", "y3", "y4", "y5", "y6", "y7", "y8"]

print(precision_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, 10))
print(recall_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevant_ids, 10))
examples.explanation: This retriever did about as well as it's mathematically possible to do: both of the only two documents that are actually relevant to this query (x1 and x2) are ranked first and second, so recall@10 comes out at a perfect 1.0 -- every relevant document that exists was found. But precision@10 is only 0.2 (2 out of 10), and that ceiling is completely unavoidable given the query only has 2 truly relevant documents anywhere in the collection -- no retriever, however good, could ever fill 10 slots with more than 2 relevant items when only 2 exist. Seeing a low precision@10 number in isolation, without checking how many relevant items actually exist for that query, would wrongly suggest this retriever is performing badly, when it's actually performing as well as is mathematically possible.

examples.title: Circular Evaluation: Why Grading Against Your Own Output Is Meaningless
examples.explanation: circular_eval treats whatever the system just returned as the relevant set, then checks the system's own results against that self-derived set -- a tautology dressed up as a measurement. Both good_results (named to suggest genuinely good results) and garbage_results (named to suggest genuinely bad, unrelated results) score an identical, perfect (1.0, 1.0) under this scheme, because any list trivially contains 100% of itself. The metric cannot tell these two completely different scenarios apart, which is exactly the tell that it isn't measuring retrieval quality at all -- it's measuring the trivial, content-free fact that a list equals itself. Genuine precision and recall require a relevant set built independently of whatever the system under test happened to return, which is exactly the discipline the next concept's golden dataset is designed to enforce.

misconceptions.description: Recall@k always means the same thing everywhere in a vector-search context, so a reported 'recall@10 of 0.97' from an ANN benchmark and a 'recall@10 of 0.97' from a retrieval-quality evaluation are directly comparable statements about the same kind of correctness.
misconceptions.clarification: The formula looks identical, but the ground truth each one is measured against is completely different. ANN recall@k compares an approximate index's results against an exact, brute-force search over the same embeddings -- it measures whether the approximation algorithm faithfully reproduces exact search, and says nothing about whether that exact search was ever returning genuinely relevant results in the first place. Retrieval-quality recall@k compares the full system's results against human-judged relevance -- it measures whether the system is actually useful, independent of how faithfully its ANN index approximates its own exact search. A system can score near-perfect on one and mediocre on the other; treating the two numbers as interchangeable statements about 'how good is this system' conflates two genuinely different questions.

misconceptions.description: A retrieval system with a low precision@k score is straightforwardly worse than one with a higher precision@k score, regardless of k or how many truly relevant items exist for the query being measured.
misconceptions.clarification: Precision@k has a hard ceiling determined by how many truly relevant items exist for a given query relative to k: if only 2 relevant items exist anywhere in the collection, precision@10 can never exceed 0.2, no matter how good the retriever is. A precision@10 of 0.2 could mean a genuinely mediocre retriever burying good results under irrelevant ones, or it could mean a retriever performing at the mathematical maximum possible for a query that simply doesn't have 10 good answers available. Comparing precision@k scores meaningfully requires accounting for how many relevant items exist per query -- either by comparing against the ceiling for that specific query, or by looking at recall@k alongside precision@k rather than precision alone.

exercises.prompt: Given 3 truly relevant documents and this ranked retrieval, what does the loop print for k = 2, 4, and 6, and what does the pattern tell you about how precision and recall behave differently as k grows?
hints: List out retrieved_ids with their positions: r1(1), x1(2), r2(3), x2(4), x3(5), r3(6) -- then for each k, count how many of the first k positions are relevant (r-prefixed).
At k=2: positions 1-2 are r1, x1 -- 1 relevant out of 2. At k=4: positions 1-4 are r1, x1, r2, x2 -- 2 relevant out of 4. At k=6: all 6 positions, all 3 r-items included -- 3 relevant out of 6.
precision divides the relevant-count by k; recall divides the same relevant-count by 3 (the total number of truly relevant documents).
exercises.solutionExplanation: At k=2, the top 2 results (r1, x1) contain exactly 1 relevant document, giving precision@2 = 1/2 = 0.5 and recall@2 = 1/3 ≈ 0.333. At k=4, the top 4 (r1, x1, r2, x2) contain 2 relevant documents, giving precision@4 = 2/4 = 0.5 (unchanged from k=2, purely by coincidence of where the relevant and irrelevant items happen to fall) and recall@4 = 2/3 ≈ 0.667 (up, since a second relevant item was found). At k=6, all 6 results are included, capturing all 3 relevant documents, giving precision@6 = 3/6 = 0.5 (still unchanged) and recall@6 = 3/3 = 1.0 (maxed out, since every relevant document has now been found). This is a deliberately constructed case where precision stays perfectly flat across all three k values while recall climbs steadily to 1.0 -- a concrete demonstration that recall is monotonically non-decreasing in k (it can only go up or stay the same as you look at more results) while precision has no such guarantee and can easily stay flat, or move in either direction, depending purely on where the relevant items happen to be ranked.

exercises.prompt: Implement precision_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k) and recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k). Then run them on the two cases below, and use the results to explain why the second case's low precision@5 does not indicate a bad retriever.
hints: Both functions follow the same shape: slice retrieved down to the first k items, count how many of those are in the relevant set, then divide by the appropriate denominator.
precision_at_k's denominator is k itself; recall_at_k's denominator is len(relevant), not k.
For case_ceiling, check how many items are actually in the 'relevant' set in total before judging whether precision@5 = 0.2 represents a flawed retriever or the best possible outcome.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For case_normal, 3 of the top 5 results (a1, a2, a3) are relevant out of 5 total, giving precision@5 = 0.6, and since all 3 relevant documents that exist were found, recall@5 = 3/3 = 1.0. For case_ceiling, only 1 of the top 5 (c1) is relevant, giving precision@5 = 1/5 = 0.2 -- but the relevant set for this case contains only 1 document total (c1), and that single relevant document is ranked first, so recall@5 = 1/1 = 1.0, a perfect score. The retriever in case_ceiling did the best it could possibly do -- it found the one and only relevant document and ranked it first -- but precision@5 is mechanically capped at 0.2 because there simply aren't 5 relevant documents available to fill those 5 slots. Reading precision@5 = 0.2 in isolation, without checking recall or how many relevant documents actually exist, would incorrectly suggest a much worse retriever than the one actually being measured here.

assessments.prompt: A benchmark reports 'HNSW recall@10 = 0.98' when comparing an approximate index against brute-force search, and a separate retrieval-quality evaluation reports 'recall@10 = 0.55' when comparing the full system's results against human relevance judgments. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: These two numbers contradict each other, so at least one of them must be measured incorrectly.

The two numbers measure different things: the ANN recall says the approximate index closely reproduces what exact search over the same embeddings would return, while the retrieval-quality recall says only about half of the genuinely relevant documents are making it into the top 10 -- a problem likely located in the embeddings, chunking, or filtering, not in the ANN algorithm itself.
The retrieval-quality recall figure must be wrong, since a properly functioning ANN index should guarantee high retrieval-quality recall too.
Both numbers measure the same underlying property, so the system's overall recall should be reported as their average.
assessments.explanation: ANN recall@k and retrieval-quality recall@k are computed against entirely different ground truths -- exact brute-force search in one case, human-judged relevance in the other -- so a system can legitimately score well on one and poorly on the other; there's no contradiction, because they're not measuring the same thing. A high ANN recall specifically rules out the approximate index as the source of a retrieval-quality problem (it's faithfully reproducing what exact search over these embeddings would find), which points investigation toward earlier stages of the pipeline -- the embedding model, how documents were chunked, or filtering logic -- as the likely source of the retrieval-quality gap. Option A and C both wrongly assume the two metrics must agree since they share a name and formula. Option D is a fabricated resolution -- averaging two numbers that answer different questions produces a number that doesn't correspond to any real, meaningful quantity.

assessments.prompt: Explain why using a retrieval system's own top-k similarity results as the 'relevant set' to evaluate that same system's precision and recall is a circular, meaningless measurement, and describe what a genuine relevance ground truth actually requires.
assessments.modelAnswer: Precision@k and recall@k are only meaningful if the 'relevant' set they're compared against was determined independently of whatever the system under test happens to output -- that independence is the entire point of the measurement, because it's what lets the metric distinguish a system that's actually finding the right documents from one that isn't. If the relevant set is instead built by taking the system's own top-k results and calling that the ground truth, the comparison collapses into checking whether a list is equal to itself, which is true by definition for absolutely any list, good or bad. A genuinely excellent retriever and a genuinely broken one that returns entirely unrelated documents would both score a perfect precision and recall of 1.0 under this scheme, because each one's output trivially matches itself -- the metric has been rendered incapable of telling them apart, which means it isn't measuring retrieval quality at all, just the tautological fact that a list contains itself. A genuine relevance ground truth has to come from a source that never looked at, and has no dependency on, the specific system's output for that query -- typically a human who independently read the underlying corpus and judged what's actually relevant, or some other trusted process kept structurally separate from the retrieval system being evaluated. This is exactly the discipline a golden or evaluation dataset is built to enforce: relevance judgments recorded once, ahead of time, independently of any particular retriever's behavior, so that measuring any retriever -- including future, changed versions of the same system -- against that fixed, independent ground truth actually means something.

concepts.title: Building a Small Evaluation (Golden) Dataset
concepts.description: Precision@k and recall@k are only as trustworthy as the relevant-item ground truth they're computed against, and that ground truth doesn't appear for free -- it has to be deliberately built, kept independent of whatever retrieval system it's used to judge, and treated as a living artifact that grows every time a real failure is discovered, rather than a one-time deliverable that gets built once at launch and never touched again.
learningObjectives: Define a golden (evaluation) dataset and explain why its relevance judgments must be produced independently of the retrieval system being measured.

Explain why a small, well-chosen golden dataset is more valuable in practice than a large one that never gets built or maintained, and describe what query-type coverage a small set should still aim for.
Describe a concrete process for sampling queries, producing relevance judgments, and deliberately including adversarial cases.
Explain the risks of using an LLM to bootstrap relevance judgments, and why human spot-checking of LLM-generated labels is still necessary.
Implement the 'every production failure becomes a new regression case' workflow and explain why it keeps a golden dataset representative over time.

sections.heading: What a Golden Dataset Actually Is, and Why Independence Matters
sections.body:
A **golden dataset** (also called an evaluation set, or a relevance benchmark) is, structurally, nothing more than a list of representative queries, each paired with the set of document or chunk ids that are genuinely relevant to that query -- exactly the `relevant` argument the precision@k and recall@k functions from the previous concept require. What makes it *golden* isn't its size or its format; it's that the relevance judgments were produced by a process kept **structurally independent** of whatever retrieval system is being measured against it.

That independence requirement rules out a specific, tempting shortcut: building the 'relevant' set by running the current retrieval system and keeping whatever it returns. As the previous concept's circular-evaluation example demonstrated concretely, that produces a tautology, not a measurement -- any system trivially matches its own output. A golden dataset's relevance judgments have to come from somewhere that never consulted the system under test: a human who independently searched or read through the underlying corpus and decided, using their own judgment, which documents actually answer a given query; a separate, deliberately-audited labeling process; or a different system altogether, so long as it's treated with appropriate skepticism (covered further down). The entire value of a golden dataset comes from this one property -- lose it, and every metric computed against it becomes meaningless, no matter how carefully the rest of the evaluation pipeline is built.

sections.heading: A Small, Well-Chosen Set Beats a Large, Neglected One
sections.body:
It's tempting to assume a golden dataset needs to be large -- hundreds or thousands of queries -- to be statistically meaningful, and that assumption quietly kills a lot of evaluation efforts before they start, because building a large, carefully human-judged dataset is a genuinely significant undertaking. The more useful framing: **a small golden dataset that actually exists and actually gets run is worth far more than a comprehensive one that never gets built, or gets built once and then abandoned.** Thirty to a hundred well-chosen queries, covering the actual variety of how the system gets used, is a completely reasonable, tractable starting point -- it's enough to catch a meaningful regression, and small enough that a team can genuinely maintain and extend it over time, which turns out to matter more than raw size (a point returned to at the end of this concept).

'Well-chosen' means covering real variety in how queries are actually phrased and what makes them hard, not just picking thirty easy, similar-looking examples. A reasonably thorough small set should include: **short, keyword-like queries** (closer to how a search bar gets used than a full sentence); **natural-language questions** phrased the way an actual user or a chatbot's user would ask them; **near-duplicate disambiguation** cases, where the collection contains two very similar documents and the query needs to surface the *correct* one specifically, not just something in the neighborhood; and **negation or precise-distinction cases**, deliberately probing the exact blind spot covered earlier in this subject -- a query that needs to distinguish 'the flight was on time' from 'the flight was not on time,' say, rather than treating anything topically nearby as good enough. A set that only contains easy, unambiguous queries will report reassuring numbers that don't reflect how the system performs on the harder queries real usage actually contains.

sections.heading: The Process: Sampling, Labeling, and Adversarial Cases
sections.body:
Building a first golden dataset follows a fairly concrete process. **Sample queries**: pull from real production query logs if the feature has already launched (the single best source, since it reflects how people actually phrase things, not how a developer imagines they would); if the feature is pre-launch, write realistic queries by hand, deliberately varying phrasing and difficulty rather than defaulting to whatever's easiest to write. **Produce relevance judgments independently**: for each sampled query, have a human -- ideally someone with real subject-matter familiarity with the underlying corpus, or failing that, the team itself for an internal tool -- read through the relevant portion of the corpus and record which documents genuinely answer the query, without ever looking at what the current retrieval system returns for it. **Deliberately include adversarial cases**: don't just wait for hard cases to occur naturally in the sample; actively construct a few queries specifically designed to be hard in the ways this subject has already covered -- near-duplicate content that needs precise disambiguation, negation pairs, rare terminology that a purely lexical approach would miss, queries where the semantically 'closest' document is a known trap rather than the right answer.

```python
golden_dataset = [
    {"query": "vacation day accrual policy", "relevant_ids": {"policy-4", "policy-4b"}},
    {"query": "refund timeline", "relevant_ids": {"faq-12"}},
    {"query": "chat support hours", "relevant_ids": {"faq-7", "faq-9"}},
]
```

Structurally, that's all a golden dataset needs to be -- a list of `{query, relevant_ids}` pairs, simple enough to store as plain JSON or CSV, and simple enough that the actual effort goes entirely into making the judgments themselves careful and independent, not into any particular storage format.

sections.heading: LLM-Assisted Labeling: A Real Accelerant, With a Real Caveat
sections.body:
Producing relevance judgments by hand doesn't scale indefinitely, and it's increasingly common to use an LLM to help bootstrap labels -- for instance, asking a model 'given this query and this candidate document, is this document relevant?' across many query/document pairs, to generate a first-pass set of judgments a human then reviews rather than produces entirely from scratch. This is a genuinely useful accelerant, and not inherently dishonest or circular *as long as the model doing the labeling is not the same model, or a model exhibiting the same blind spots, as the retrieval system being evaluated* -- otherwise this reintroduces a milder version of the exact circularity problem from the previous concept.

The caveat that actually matters in practice: an LLM-based (or any automated) labeler is not automatically trustworthy just because it's more sophisticated than the retrieval system it's helping evaluate, and it can inherit the exact same kinds of blind spots this subject has already covered.

```python
def toy_llm_labeler(query, candidate_text):
    # A deliberately simplified stand-in for a labeling model's judgment,
    # using lexical overlap -- real labelers are far more sophisticated,
    # but can still share the same underlying blind spot demonstrated here.
    query_words = set(query.lower().split())
    candidate_words = set(candidate_text.lower().split())
    overlap = len(query_words & candidate_words) / len(query_words)
    return overlap > 0.5

query = "was the flight on time"
candidate_a = "The flight was on time."
candidate_b = "The flight was NOT on time."

print(toy_llm_labeler(query, candidate_a))   # True -- correctly relevant
print(toy_llm_labeler(query, candidate_b))   # True -- WRONGLY labeled relevant too
```

Both candidates score as 'relevant' under this simplified labeler, because negation is a single word buried inside overwhelming surface-level overlap -- exactly the blind spot covered earlier in this subject for embedding models, resurfacing here in a labeling context. A production LLM labeler is considerably better than this toy stand-in, but is not immune to the same category of mistake, especially on exactly the adversarial cases (negation, precise factual distinctions) a golden dataset most needs to get right. The practical rule: use LLM assistance to accelerate the *first draft* of labels, but always have a human spot-check a meaningful sample of the results -- especially the adversarial cases -- before trusting them as ground truth.

sections.heading: Treat It Like Code: Versioning and Growing It Over Time

examples.title: A Tiny Golden Dataset and an Aggregate Evaluation Harness
examples.explanation: stub_retrieve stands in for a real retrieval pipeline, returning a fixed, pre-determined ranking for each of the three queries -- in practice this would be a real call into the embedding model and ANN index instead. evaluate loops over every case in the golden dataset, computes precision@3 and recall@3 for each one individually, and averages both across the whole set: the vacation-policy query gets 2 of its 2 relevant documents into the top 3 (precision 2/3, recall 1.0), the refund query gets 1 of its 1 relevant document (precision 1/3, recall 1.0), and the support-hours query gets 2 of its 2 relevant documents (precision 2/3, recall 1.0) -- averaging to about 0.556 precision and a perfect 1.0 recall across the whole three-query set. This is the mechanical core of an evaluation harness: a fixed, independently-labeled golden dataset, run through whatever retrieval function is currently being tested, producing a single aggregate number that can be compared against a previous run.

examples.title: An LLM-Style Labeler Can Inherit the Exact Same Negation Blind Spot
examples.code:
def toy_llm_labeler(query, candidate_text):
    query_words = set(query.lower().split())
    candidate_words = set(candidate_text.lower().split())
    overlap = len(query_words & candidate_words) / len(query_words)
    return overlap > 0.5

query = "was the flight on time"
candidate_a = "The flight was on time."
candidate_b = "The flight was NOT on time."

print(toy_llm_labeler(query, candidate_a))
print(toy_llm_labeler(query, candidate_b))
examples.explanation: This deliberately simplified labeler decides relevance purely by lexical word overlap -- a stand-in for the general risk that any automated labeling process, however sophisticated, can be fooled by surface-level similarity. candidate_a genuinely is relevant, and correctly gets labeled True. candidate_b describes the opposite outcome (the flight was NOT on time) but shares every other word with the query, so it also gets labeled True -- an incorrect relevance judgment that a human reading both sentences side by side would never make. If this kind of mislabeled case made it into a golden dataset unreviewed, every future evaluation run would silently reward a retriever for treating these two opposite-meaning sentences as equally relevant, baking a wrong assumption permanently into the ground truth itself -- exactly why LLM-assisted labeling needs human spot-checking, especially on precisely the adversarial cases (negation, precise distinctions) it's most likely to get wrong.

examples.title: Turning a Discovered Failure Into a Permanent Regression Case
examples.explanation: Before the regression case is added, the golden dataset only contains q1, which retrieve_current handles correctly (d1 is in its top 3), so avg_recall reports a perfectly reassuring 1.0 -- but that number is reassuring only because the dataset has never asked about the case that's actually broken. A user reports that q2 should have surfaced d4, and add_regression_case records that as a permanent new entry in the golden dataset. Re-running the exact same avg_recall function against the exact same still-unfixed retrieve_current now correctly drops to 0.5, because retrieve_current's response for q2 (d5, d6, d7) never includes d4 -- the golden dataset's aggregate score now honestly reflects the known gap instead of hiding it. This one new entry stays in the dataset permanently: it will correctly report a passing 1.0 again the moment a real fix ships, and it will keep silently catching any future change that reintroduces the same failure, which is the entire point of converting a one-off bug report into a permanent, automatically-checked test case.

misconceptions.description: A golden dataset only needs to be built once, at launch; after that, the initial set of queries and judgments remains a valid way to measure retrieval quality indefinitely.
misconceptions.clarification: A golden dataset's usefulness comes from how representative it is of real usage and real failure modes, and both of those drift over time -- new document categories get added, real query patterns shift as the user base or product changes, and production failures surface gaps the original sample never anticipated. A dataset frozen at launch slowly stops reflecting reality, reporting numbers that look stable purely because it's no longer asking about the cases that would actually reveal a problem. Treating it as a living artifact -- adding a new permanent case every time a real failure is discovered, the same discipline as adding a regression test for every bug fix in software generally -- is what keeps its numbers meaningful years after launch, not a one-time build effort.

misconceptions.description: Having an LLM generate relevance judgments for a golden dataset is just as trustworthy as a human doing it, since the LLM is more capable than the embedding model or retrieval system actually being evaluated.
misconceptions.clarification: Being more capable than the system under test doesn't make a labeling model immune to the same categories of mistake that system might make -- a labeler relying heavily on surface-level lexical or semantic similarity can mislabel exactly the adversarial cases (negation, precise factual distinctions, near-duplicate disambiguation) a golden dataset most needs to get right, the same blind spot that shows up in embedding-based retrieval itself. LLM assistance is a legitimate way to accelerate producing a first draft of labels at scale, but the resulting judgments still need a human to spot-check a meaningful sample -- especially the hardest, most adversarial cases -- before they're trusted as ground truth; skipping that check risks baking a wrong assumption permanently into the very foundation every future evaluation run depends on.

exercises.prompt: Using the same golden dataset and stub retriever as the aggregate-evaluation example above, but evaluated at k=2 instead of k=3, what does the final print statement output?
hints: At k=2, only the first 2 items of each query's fixed result list matter -- work out stub_retrieve's top-2 for each of the three queries individually first.
For the vacation-policy query, the top 2 are policy-4 and policy-2 -- only policy-4 is relevant, so that case scores 1 hit out of 2 possible relevant documents.
Compute precision (hits/2) and recall (hits/total relevant for that case) for all three cases individually, then average each metric separately across the three cases.
exercises.solutionExplanation: At k=2: the vacation-policy query's top 2 (policy-4, policy-2) contain 1 of its 2 relevant documents -- precision 1/2=0.5, recall 1/2=0.5. The refund query's top 2 (faq-3, faq-12) contain 1 of its 1 relevant document -- precision 1/2=0.5, recall 1/1=1.0. The support-hours query's top 2 (faq-7, faq-2) contain 1 of its 2 relevant documents -- precision 1/2=0.5, recall 1/2=0.5. Averaging precision across the three cases gives (0.5+0.5+0.5)/3=0.5, and averaging recall gives (0.5+1.0+0.5)/3≈0.6667. Every case happens to land on exactly the same precision (0.5) at this k, purely because each query's top 2 always contains exactly 1 hit -- but recall varies per case because the total number of relevant documents differs between queries (1 for refund, 2 for the other two).

exercises.prompt: Implement add_regression_case(golden_dataset, query, relevant_ids) so it appends a new case to the dataset. Then use it to add a newly-discovered failure (query 'q3' should have relevant_ids {'c1'}) to the existing 2-case dataset below, and print the average recall@3 (using retrieve_buggy) before and after adding it.
hints: add_regression_case just needs to build a dict shaped like the existing entries in golden_dataset and append it -- golden_dataset.append({"query": query, "relevant_ids": set(relevant_ids)}).
Before adding q3, the dataset only knows about q1 (fully correct, recall 1.0) and q2 (partially correct -- b2 is missing from retrieve_buggy's response, recall 0.5).
After adding q3, retrieve_buggy's response for q3 (c2, c3, c4) never includes the truly relevant c1 -- that case scores recall 0.0, pulling the average down further.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Before add_regression_case runs, the 2-case dataset scores an average recall of 0.75: q1 gets a perfect 1.0 (a1 is in retrieve_buggy's top 3), and q2 gets 0.5 (only b1 of its 2 relevant documents -- b1 and b2 -- appears in the top 3, since b3 and b4 aren't actually relevant). After add_regression_case appends the q3 case, the average drops to 0.5, because q3's newly-added relevant document (c1) never appears anywhere in retrieve_buggy's response for q3 (c2, c3, c4) -- a recall of 0.0 for that case, dragging the three-case average down from 0.75 to (1.0+0.5+0.0)/3=0.5. The dataset's measured quality dropped not because the retriever changed at all, but because the dataset now knows to ask about a failure it previously had no way to detect -- exactly the intended effect of converting a discovered bug into a permanent case.

assessments.prompt: A team building their first golden dataset for a new RAG feature decides to construct relevance judgments by running their current retrieval system on each sampled query and recording whatever it returns as the 'relevant' set. What's wrong with this approach?
options: Nothing is wrong -- this is an efficient way to bootstrap a golden dataset without needing manual human review.

It produces a circular, tautological measurement: the relevant set is derived from the very system being evaluated, so that system (and any equally bad system with the same output) will always score a perfect precision and recall against it, regardless of whether its results are actually good.
This approach works fine as long as the retrieval system uses cosine similarity rather than dot product.
The main problem is that this approach is too slow to scale to a large number of queries.
assessments.explanation: A golden dataset's relevance judgments must be produced independently of the system being measured, precisely so the metric can distinguish a genuinely good system from a genuinely bad one. Deriving the relevant set from the system's own output collapses that distinction entirely -- any system's results trivially match themselves, so precision and recall against a self-derived ground truth are always perfect, telling you nothing about actual retrieval quality. Option A misidentifies this as merely an efficiency shortcut rather than a fundamental measurement flaw. Option C is a fabricated, irrelevant condition -- the choice of similarity metric has no bearing on this circularity problem. Option D is wrong for a different reason -- speed isn't the issue here; the approach is fast precisely because it isn't actually measuring anything.

assessments.prompt: Describe an end-to-end process for creating a first golden dataset for a brand-new RAG feature that has no production query logs yet, including how you'd make sure it actually catches real problems rather than just reporting reassuring numbers.
assessments.modelAnswer: With no production logs to sample from, the first step is writing realistic queries by hand, deliberately varying both phrasing style and difficulty rather than defaulting to whatever's easiest to think of -- a mix of short, keyword-like queries closer to search-bar usage, and fuller natural-language questions closer to how a chatbot user would actually type. Alongside that organic sample, deliberately construct a handful of adversarial cases targeting the specific failure modes this subject has already covered: at least one negation pair (two near-identical sentences with opposite meaning), at least one near-duplicate disambiguation case (two very similar documents where only one is actually the correct answer), and at least one case using rare or domain-specific terminology a purely lexical match would miss. For every query in the resulting set, produce relevance judgments independently of the retrieval system itself -- ideally by having someone with real familiarity with the underlying corpus read through it directly and record which documents genuinely answer the query, without ever looking at what the retrieval system currently returns; LLM assistance can accelerate this first pass, but only if a human spot-checks a meaningful sample of the results afterward, especially the adversarial cases, since an automated labeler can inherit the same blind spots (like the negation issue) that the retrieval system itself might have. Store the resulting {query, relevant_ids} pairs as a simple, versioned, structured artifact in the same repository as the retrieval code, and run precision@k and recall@k against it as a matter of routine whenever anything that could affect retrieval changes -- a new embedding model, a chunking change, an index parameter tweak. Most importantly, treat launch as the beginning, not the end: every time a real user-facing failure surfaces in production, add it as a new permanent case via something like add_regression_case, so the golden dataset keeps growing to reflect the actual failure modes the system has, rather than staying frozen at whatever the team happened to imagine before the feature ever shipped.

concepts.title: Why 'It Looks Right When I Try It' Isn't Enough
concepts.description: Manually typing a few queries and eyeballing whether the results seem reasonable feels like validation, but it's biased in specific, predictable ways -- it tests easy queries, it can't perceive the relevant documents that should have shown up and didn't, and it never runs again automatically before the next change ships -- and for a RAG system, the final output is a fluent LLM answer that looks even more convincing than a raw list of search results, one more layer removed from whether retrieval actually worked.
learningObjectives: Identify the specific cognitive biases behind manual spot-checking of retrieval results: query selection bias, small-sample luck, and the inability to perceive false negatives.

Explain why a fluent, confident RAG chatbot answer is an even weaker signal of retrieval correctness than a raw search result list looking reasonable, and connect this to the RAG-hallucination content from earlier in this subject.
Explain why manual spot-checking provides no protection against a regression introduced by a later change, unlike an automated golden-dataset evaluation.
Describe a layered validation strategy combining offline golden-dataset evaluation, production monitoring signals, and periodic random-sample manual review.
Diagnose, given a specific scenario, whether a validation failure is due to query selection bias, an unmeasured false negative, or a missing regression check.

sections.heading: The Specific Biases Behind Manual Spot-Checking
sections.body:
Trying a handful of queries by hand and checking whether the results 'look reasonable' feels like due diligence, and it isn't worthless -- but it's worth being precise about exactly how it's biased, because the biases are specific and predictable rather than random noise that averages out.

**Query selection bias**: the person doing the manual check is almost always the developer who built the system, or someone deeply familiar with the underlying corpus -- and that familiarity unconsciously steers them toward typing queries using the same vocabulary the documents themselves use, because that's the vocabulary in their head. Real users don't share that vocabulary; they paraphrase, they use casual or imprecise language, they ask questions the developer would never think to ask because the developer already knows the answer. A system that looks excellent against developer-style queries can perform meaningfully worse against the actual distribution of real user phrasing, and manual testing structurally can't reveal that gap, because it's drawing its test queries from the same biased source every time.

**Small-sample luck**: trying three, five, or even ten queries by hand is a tiny, non-random sample, and a tiny sample can look great by chance even when the system's true performance across realistic traffic is mediocre -- one anecdote, or even several, is not a distribution, and treating it like one systematically overstates confidence.

**Can't perceive false negatives**: this is the subtlest and most consequential bias. When a human looks at a list of returned results and judges whether the top one 'looks relevant,' they're evaluating what's in front of them -- they have no way to notice a document that *should* have been returned but wasn't, because that document, by definition, isn't visible in the results being reviewed. A near-miss wrong result that's topically adjacent to the right answer looks perfectly plausible on casual inspection -- exactly the clustered, plausible-looking failure mode covered when this subject discussed ANN recall and embedding blind spots -- so a manual reviewer systematically fails to catch precisely the failures that look most benign.

sections.heading: Two Layers Removed: When the Output Is a Fluent LLM Answer
sections.body:
For a RAG system specifically, manual validation gets even less reliable, because what a human reviewer typically looks at isn't the raw retrieved chunks -- it's the LLM's final, generated answer. This is directly connected to the RAG-hallucination content covered earlier in this subject: an LLM has no way to know whether the context it was handed is actually relevant, and a capable model will confidently, fluently synthesize a plausible-sounding answer from mediocre or wrong context just as readily as from good context. A well-written, confident-sounding chatbot response is therefore an even weaker signal of retrieval correctness than a raw list of search results looking reasonable -- it's an extra layer removed, filtered through a component (the LLM) whose entire job is to produce fluent, plausible-sounding text regardless of whether the underlying material actually supports it.

This produces a specific, dangerous failure pattern: a stakeholder or reviewer tries the chatbot, gets a well-written, confident answer, and reasonably (but wrongly) concludes 'this works.' The fluency of the answer has almost nothing to do with whether the retrieval step underneath actually found the right documents -- a model can write an equally confident, equally fluent sentence from the right context or the wrong context, and a casual reviewer reading only the final answer has no way to tell which one happened. Validating a RAG system by reading its answers is validating the wrong layer of the pipeline; the actual thing that needs checking is what got retrieved, not how well the model wrote about it afterward.

sections.heading: No Regression Protection Without Automation
A Layered Validation Strategy That Actually Catches Problems
sections.body:
None of this means manual review is worthless -- it means manual review of a small, hand-picked sample can't be the *only* line of defense, and needs to be combined with mechanisms that don't share its blind spots. A genuinely robust validation strategy layers three distinct mechanisms, each catching what the others miss:

**Offline batch evaluation against the golden dataset** (the previous concept), run automatically whenever anything that could affect retrieval changes -- this is the mechanism with actual regression protection, since it reruns the same fixed, independently-labeled cases every time, catching exactly the kind of silent degradation the example above demonstrates.

**Production monitoring signals**, tracked continuously on live traffic rather than a fixed offline set -- a **zero-result rate** (the fraction of real queries that come back with nothing after filtering, a direct, measurable red flag with no need for relevance labels at all), a query-reformulation or rephrase rate (a proxy for users not finding what they wanted the first time), and any explicit feedback signal (thumbs-down, a support ticket) that's available. These catch problems the golden dataset doesn't yet know to look for, in as close to real time as the system allows.

```python
def zero_result_rate(query_log):
    zero_count = sum(1 for entry in query_log if entry["num_results"] == 0)
    return zero_count / len(query_log)
```

**Periodic manual review of a genuinely random sample of real production queries and their retrieved results** -- deliberately not hand-picked ones, and reviewing the actual retrieved chunks, not just a chatbot's final generated answer -- specifically to hunt for failure categories the golden dataset doesn't yet cover. Anything this random review turns up that represents a real, previously-unknown failure mode feeds directly back into the golden dataset via the regression-case workflow from the previous concept, closing the loop: manual review's role shifts from 'the only check' (where its biases go uncorrected) to 'the mechanism that discovers new blind spots for the automated checks to permanently cover from then on.'

examples.title: Developer Vocabulary vs. Real User Phrasing: The Same Retriever, Two Very Different Scores
examples.code:
def recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k):
    top_k = retrieved[:k]
    hits = sum(1 for item in top_k if item in relevant)
    return hits / len(relevant)

docs = {
    "d1": "Employees accrue vacation days monthly.",
    "d2": "Refunds are processed within five business days.",
    "d3": "Support is available via chat at all hours.",
}

def toy_retrieve(query, k):
    # A deliberately simple lexical-overlap retriever, standing in for any
    # retrieval system that only partially handles paraphrase.
    query_words = set(query.lower().replace(".", "").split())
    scores = []
    for doc_id, text in docs.items():
        doc_words = set(text.lower().replace(".", "").split())
        scores.append((doc_id, len(query_words & doc_words)))
    scores.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)
    return [doc_id for doc_id, _ in scores[:k]]

developer_queries = [
    {"query": "employees accrue vacation days", "relevant_ids": {"d1"}},
    {"query": "refunds processed business days", "relevant_ids": {"d2"}},
    {"query": "support available chat hours", "relevant_ids": {"d3"}},
]
real_user_queries = [
    {"query": "how much time off do I earn per month", "relevant_ids": {"d1"}},
    {"query": "when will I get my money back", "relevant_ids": {"d2"}},
    {"query": "can I talk to someone right now", "relevant_ids": {"d3"}},
]

def avg_recall(dataset, retrieve_fn, k):
    scores = [recall_at_k(retrieve_fn(c["query"], k), c["relevant_ids"], k) for c in dataset]
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

print(round(avg_recall(developer_queries, toy_retrieve, 1), 3))
print(round(avg_recall(real_user_queries, toy_retrieve, 1), 3))
examples.explanation: The developer_queries deliberately reuse the exact same words the documents themselves contain -- exactly the vocabulary a developer testing their own system tends to reach for -- and this lexical-overlap retriever scores a perfect 1.0 average recall@1 against them, because there's always strong, direct word overlap with the correct document. real_user_queries ask for the same underlying information but phrased the way an actual person might, sharing essentially no literal vocabulary with any of the three documents at all -- with zero lexical overlap against every document, the retriever has no real signal to work with and effectively falls back to an arbitrary tie-break, scoring only 0.333 average recall@1 across the same three underlying questions. Nothing about the retriever changed between the two evaluations -- only which queries were used to test it -- and that alone was enough to swing the measured quality from 'looks perfect' to 'mostly wrong.' A developer who only ever tries queries phrased the way they themselves would phrase them will systematically see the first number, not the second, and walk away with unwarranted confidence.

examples.title: A False Negative Invisible to Anyone Only Looking at the Top 3
examples.explanation: Two documents are genuinely relevant to this query: item1 (ranked first) and item7 (ranked seventh). A human reviewer glancing at only the top 3 results sees item1 present and reasonably concludes the system is working well -- but item7 is nowhere in that window ('item7' in manual_review_window is False), so the reviewer has no way to even suspect a second relevant document exists and is being systematically excluded from what they're looking at. recall@3 (0.5) quantifies exactly this gap -- half of the truly relevant documents for this query aren't making it into a realistic display window -- while recall@10 (1.0) confirms the document does exist and is findable, just further down than a casual glance would ever reach. This is the false-negative blind spot made concrete: nothing about eyeballing the visible top 3 could have revealed that a relevant document was being missed, because the very thing that needs noticing is, by construction, not visible in what's being reviewed.

examples.title: A Regression the Manual Spot-Check Misses, but the Full Golden Set Catches
examples.explanation: A developer manually re-checks queries q1 and q2 after some change -- an index parameter tweak, say -- and both still work perfectly, giving the manual_subset an average recall@1 of a perfectly reassuring 1.0. Nothing about that spot check was done carelessly; it's just an incomplete sample. Running the exact same retrieve_current against the full 5-query golden_dataset instead reveals that q3, q4, and q5 are now all broken (each retrieving an unrelated 'x' item instead of its actual relevant document), dropping the true average recall@1 to 0.4 -- a real, significant regression that the manually-checked two queries happened to be entirely blind to. The developer's spot check wasn't wrong about q1 and q2; it was simply never capable of revealing a problem in q3 through q5, because it never looked at them -- which is exactly why an automated check against the full, fixed golden set catches regressions that a necessarily partial, ad hoc manual sample structurally cannot.

misconceptions.description: If a developer tries a handful of realistic-sounding queries themselves and the results look reasonable, that's sufficient validation before shipping a retrieval change.
misconceptions.clarification: Manual spot-checking carries specific, predictable biases that don't average out with a little more care: the queries a developer thinks to try tend to share vocabulary with the underlying documents in a way real users' queries don't, a handful of tried queries is too small a sample to represent real traffic, and a human reviewing visible results has no way to notice a relevant document that should have appeared but didn't, since that omission isn't visible in what's being reviewed. None of this means manual testing is useless -- it means it needs to be paired with an automated evaluation against an independently-labeled golden dataset (which reruns the same fixed cases every time, catching regressions a one-off manual sample can't) and with production monitoring signals that reveal problems the golden dataset doesn't yet cover.

misconceptions.description: If a RAG chatbot's final answer reads fluently and confidently, the retrieval step that fed it context must have worked correctly.
misconceptions.clarification: An LLM generating the final answer has no way to know whether the context it was handed is actually relevant, and a capable model will write an equally fluent, confident-sounding answer from good context or from mediocre, wrong context -- fluency is a property of the language model's writing ability, not evidence about what was actually retrieved underneath it. Validating a RAG system by reading its final answers is checking a layer of the pipeline that's specifically designed to sound convincing regardless of input quality; the layer that actually needs checking is what got retrieved -- the raw chunks handed to the model -- not how persuasively the model wrote about whatever it was given.

exercises.prompt: A developer manually re-checks only queries q1 and q2 after a retrieval change, while the full golden dataset covers q1 through q5. What does each print statement output, and what does the difference reveal?
hints: Check retrieve_current's response for each of the 5 queries against its expected relevant_ids ({'d1'} for q1, {'d2'} for q2, and so on) -- which ones actually return their correct document?
manual_subset only ever contains the q1 and q2 cases, both of which retrieve_current handles correctly -- what recall does a dataset made entirely of correct cases report?

The full golden_dataset includes q3, q4, and q5 as well, none of which retrieve_current answers correctly (each returns an unrelated 'x'-prefixed item) -- average recall across all 5 cases, 2 correct and 3 incorrect.
exercises.solutionExplanation: retrieve_current correctly returns d1 for q1 and d2 for q2, so manual_subset -- containing only those two cases -- scores a perfect average recall@1 of 1.0. But retrieve_current returns x3, x4, and x5 for q3, q4, and q5 respectively, none of which match those queries' actual relevant documents (d3, d4, d5) -- each of those three cases scores recall 0.0. Averaging recall across all 5 cases in the full golden_dataset gives (1.0+1.0+0.0+0.0+0.0)/5 = 0.4, revealing that 3 of the 5 query patterns are now completely broken -- a real, significant regression the manual_subset was structurally incapable of detecting, since it never looked at any of the three broken cases in the first place.

exercises.prompt: Write zero_result_rate(query_log) that returns the fraction of entries in query_log whose 'num_results' is exactly 0. Then run it on the sample production query log below and interpret whether the resulting rate would be considered a healthy or concerning signal.
exercises.code:

    pass

Divide that count by len(query_log) to get a fraction between 0 and 1.

This signal needs no relevance labels at all -- it's purely observing how often real users get literally nothing back, which is exactly why it can run continuously on live traffic rather than only against a fixed offline golden dataset.
exercises.solutionCode:
def zero_result_rate(query_log):
    zero_count = sum(1 for entry in query_log if entry["num_results"] == 0)
    return zero_count / len(query_log)


query_log = [
    {"query": "vacation days", "num_results": 5},
    {"query": "obscure config flag xyz123", "num_results": 0},
    {"query": "refund policy", "num_results": 3},
    {"query": "asdkjaskjd", "num_results": 0},
    {"query": "chat support", "num_results": 4},
    {"query": "internal codename banana", "num_results": 0},
    {"query": "sick leave", "num_results": 2},
    {"query": "printer setup", "num_results": 1},

exercises.solutionExplanation: Three of the eight logged queries came back with zero results (the config-flag query, the keyboard-mashed query, and the internal-codename query), giving zero_result_rate = 3/8 = 0.375. Whether 37.5% is 'healthy' depends on context this single number can't fully answer on its own -- some of these zero-result queries are arguably reasonable (a keyboard-mashed string genuinely has no relevant documents), while others might indicate a real gap (an internal codename a user reasonably expects to find something about). This is exactly why zero_result_rate is best used as a production monitoring signal that gets watched over time for trend changes and gets spot-checked case by case, rather than a single offline pass/fail gate -- a sudden jump in this rate after a deploy is a strong, fast, ground-truth-free early warning worth investigating immediately, distinct from and complementary to the periodic, deeper golden-dataset evaluation.

assessments.prompt: A developer manually tries several queries against a retrieval system and concludes it's working well because every result they see looks relevant. Why does this kind of manual check systematically tend to miss false negatives (relevant documents that should have been retrieved but weren't)?
options: Manual checks are just as good at catching false negatives as automated evaluation, as long as the developer is careful.

A human reviewing a list of returned results can only judge what's actually visible in front of them; a relevant document that should have appeared but didn't is, by definition, not present in that list, so there's nothing in the reviewer's field of view to prompt them to notice its absence.
False negatives only occur when the embedding model is outdated, which a manual check can always detect by inspecting the model's version number.
Manual checks miss false negatives only when the reviewer is unfamiliar with the underlying corpus.
assessments.explanation: A false negative's defining characteristic is that it's a document that should be in the results but isn't -- there's no representation of 'the thing that's missing' anywhere in what a reviewer is actually looking at, so nothing prompts them to go looking for it. This is a structural limitation of reviewing visible output, independent of how careful or diligent the reviewer is, which is exactly why option A is wrong -- more care doesn't create visibility into something that isn't there. Option C invents an unrelated, narrow cause (model staleness) as if it were the general explanation. Option D is also wrong -- even a reviewer deeply familiar with the corpus faces the same structural blind spot, since familiarity with the corpus doesn't make an absent result visible in the list being reviewed.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says the RAG chatbot 'must be retrieving fine' because its answers read fluently and confidently. Explain why that reasoning is unreliable and what you'd check instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fluency and confidence are properties of the language model's writing ability, not evidence about the quality of the context it was given -- an LLM generating an answer has no built-in way to detect that its retrieved context is irrelevant or wrong, and a capable model will synthesize an equally well-written, equally confident-sounding response whether the underlying chunks actually support the answer or not. This is the same failure mode covered earlier in this subject when discussing RAG hallucinations: a confidently wrong answer and a confidently correct one can look identical from the outside, because the model's fluency doesn't come with any signal distinguishing which case actually occurred. Judging retrieval quality by reading the chatbot's final answers is therefore checking the wrong layer of the pipeline -- it's two steps removed from the thing that actually needs validating, filtered first through whatever the retrieval step happened to find and then through the generation step's tendency to sound plausible regardless. What I'd check instead is the actual retrieved context for a representative set of queries: pull the raw chunks that were handed to the model for several real (ideally randomly sampled, not hand-picked) queries, and verify directly whether those chunks actually contain the information needed to answer correctly -- independent of how the model went on to phrase its response. Beyond that spot check, I'd want the same layered approach covered in this concept: an automated evaluation of retrieval (not final answers) against an independently-labeled golden dataset that reruns on every relevant change, plus production signals like zero-result rate that don't depend on reading any generated text at all. Confident-sounding output is, at best, a signal about the language model; it's not a substitute for actually checking what retrieval handed it.
